citation.title: Field Experimental Designs for the Study of Media Effects

standing_assumptions:
The article (Political Communication 31:168–180, 2014; PDF pp. 2–14, PDF p. 1 being the publisher's cover page) is an overview of experimental designs. It has no theorem, no displayed formula, no mathematical notation, no table or figure and no formal model; every statistical claim is made in words. The setting those claims inherit, as printed (read from the page images):
[Basic design and its assumptions: section ‘Between-Subjects Design’, p. 170 (PDF p. 4)] “The most basic experimental design is one in which subjects are assigned individually and with identical probability to treatment or control conditions. Assuming that (a) the random assignments are implemented as planned and outcomes are observed for all subjects, (b) the only systematic factor that causes the treatment group to differ from the control group is the intended treatment, and (c) subjects respond solely to the treatment that they receive (and are unaffected by treatments administered to others), the between-subjects design provides the basis for unbiased estimation of the average causal effect of the treatment in the subject pool (Gerber & Green, 2012). Indeed, the estimation of the average causal effect is simple and intuitive: The average outcome in the control group is subtracted from the average outcome in the treatment group.”
[Clustered design: section ‘Between-Subjects Clustered Design’, p. 171 (PDF p. 5)] “Accordingly, researchers studying the effects of TV or radio randomly assign their treatments to geographic clusters. In effect, all individuals living within the same geographic cluster are assigned together to either treatment or control conditions. In the between-subjects clustered design, clusters are assigned independently, but individuals within clusters are not.”
[Estimand under clustering: p. 172 (PDF p. 6)] “The design suggestions given above presuppose that a researcher’s aim in conducting a clustered experiment is the estimation of an \emph{individual-level} average treatment effect.”
[Randomization inference: p. 172 (PDF p. 6)] “One option in such settings is hypothesis testing based on the method of randomization inference (Fisher, 1935; Rosenbaum, 2002). Under the null hypothesis of no treatment effect whatsoever, one may simulate the sampling distribution of possible estimated treatment effects under all possible random assignments. The $p$ value of the observed estimate is calculated based on its location relative to this randomization distribution.”
[No interference: Note 2, p. 177 (PDF p. 11), attached on p. 171 to the discussion of spillovers in Bond et al.] “2. Modeling spillovers in this way in effect relaxes the assumption that subjects are affected solely by their own treatment status and not the status of others.”
Not stated anywhere in the article: potential-outcome notation; a formula for any estimator; an assignment mechanism beyond the words quoted (complete randomization of a fixed number of units and independent assignment with a common probability both fit “assigned individually and with identical probability” and “clusters are assigned independently”); a sequence of populations for the consistency statement, or any bound on outcomes or on cluster sizes; a sampling model. The formal renderings in the targets below are therefore the audit's, taken from the validators' derivations and from the two readers' exact checks, in finite-population potential-outcome notation: units $i = 1, \ldots, N$ with fixed potential outcomes $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$; an assignment $Z \in \{0,1\}^N$ that is the only source of randomness (the article's condition (b)); observed outcome $Y_i = Z_iY_i(1) + (1-Z_i)Y_i(0)$ for every unit (conditions (a) and (c)); average effect $\tau = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i [Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]$.
What is and is not a target. Two findings are confirmed errors whose correction changes a mathematical statement: P024-A002 (Moderate; p. 174, the stated necessity of a no-other-change assumption under randomized timing) and P024-E002 (Minor; p. 171, consistency stated without a regularity condition). Each has a counterexample and a corrected statement below. P024-E001 (Moderate) is not a target: it is a misreported statistic from a cited study (p. 171 gives the Bond et al. (2012) effect as approximately 0.7 percentage points where the source reports 0.39), a reporting finding with no mathematical statement to correct, and no claim of the article is derived from the number. The other sixteen error-class findings (P024-E005 to P024-E016, P024-N001, P024-N003, P024-N007, P024-N008) are citation, reference-list, spelling and grammar misprints. Of the nine headline claims, P024-H2, P024-H3 and P024-H5 contain a mathematical statement (unbiasedness; bias and consistency; a weighted-average identity) and are targets; P024-H1, P024-H4, P024-H6, P024-H8 and P024-H9 are framing, qualitative or practical claims; the formal content of P024-H7 (sharp-null randomization tests under a randomized schedule) is part (b) of P024-T2.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Single-Medium Multi-Outcome Crossover Design’, first paragraph, sentence beginning ‘In order to attribute a change in outcomes to the treatment’, as printed; the witness is the validator's construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement refuted: p. 174 (PDF p. 8)] “One alternative is to deploy a within-subjects design that randomizes the timing of the treatment. This approach can be informative, but it relies on fairly strong assumptions (see Gerber & Green, 2012, chapter 8). In order to attribute a change in outcomes to the treatment, one must assume that the treatment is the sole systematic factor that changes over time.” [Reading refuted] For the randomized-timing design of the preceding sentence, causal attribution (a design-unbiased estimate of an average effect, or a valid test of the sharp null of no effect) requires that the untreated outcome not change systematically over time. [Witness: validator's construction, not in the paper] One media outlet; calendar periods $t = 1, 2, 3, 4$; one outcome per period; one intervention that is permanent from its onset. The onset $S$ is drawn uniformly from $\{2, 3, 4\}$ and is the only randomness; $Z_t(s) = \mathbf{1}\{t \ge s\}$. For every onset $s \in \{2, 3, 4\}$ and every period $t$ the potential outcome is $$Y_t(s) = t^2 + 2\,\mathbf{1}\{t \ge s\},$$ so that the outcome depends on the schedule only through current exposure (no anticipation, no carryover), with untreated values $Y_t(0) = t^2$, that is $(1, 4, 9, 16)$, and treated values $Y_t(1) = t^2 + 2$, that is $(3, 6, 11, 18)$. The observed outcome in period $t$ is $Y_t = Y_t(S)$, and all four are observed. The exposure probabilities are $p_t = \Pr(Z_t(S) = 1) = (0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)$ for $t = 1, \ldots, 4$. [Claims] (i) [The treatment is not the sole systematic factor that changes over time.] The untreated outcome $t^2$ is not constant in $t$: it is $1, 4, 9, 16$ whatever the onset. (ii) [A design-unbiased effect estimator exists.] Let $\tau = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=2}^{3}[Y_t(1) - Y_t(0)] = 2$ and $$\widehat{\tau}(S) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=2}^{3}\left\{\frac{Z_t(S)\,Y_t}{p_t} - \frac{[1 - Z_t(S)]\,Y_t}{1 - p_t}\right\}.$$ Then $\widehat{\tau}(2) = 69/4$, $\widehat{\tau}(3) = 21/4$, $\widehat{\tau}(4) = -33/2$, and $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau}(S)] = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{69}{4} + \frac{21}{4} - \frac{33}{2}\right) = 2 = \tau$. Its variance is $1561/8$. (iii) [A valid sharp-null test exists.] Replace the potential outcomes by $Y_t(s) = t^2$ for every $s$ (no effect of any kind, the same trend). For the before-after statistic $$D(s) = \frac{1}{5-s}\sum_{t=s}^{4} t^2 - \frac{1}{s-1}\sum_{t=1}^{s-1} t^2,$$ $D(2) = 26/3$, $D(3) = 10$, $D(4) = 34/3$. The randomization $p$-value $p(s) = \#\{u \in \{2,3,4\} : D(u) \ge D(s)\}/3$ takes the values $p(2) = 1$, $p(3) = 2/3$, $p(4) = 1/3$, so $\Pr(p(S) \le k/3) = k/3$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, 3$ and $\Pr(p(S) \le \alpha) \le \alpha$ for every $\alpha \in [0, 1]$. (iv) [Consequence.] There is a single-outlet within-subjects design with randomized timing, with all outcomes observed and the schedule the only randomness, in which the treatment is not the sole systematic factor that changes over time and yet (ii) and (iii) hold. The assumption is therefore not necessary for causal attribution under that design.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: “a within-subjects design that randomizes the timing of the treatment” for “just a single media outlet” (p. 174, PDF p. 8); the paper gives no notation, estimator, schedule distribution or definition of ‘systematic factor’ for it. The sharp null (p. 172, PDF p. 6: “the null hypothesis of no treatment effect whatsoever”; p. 174, PDF p. 8: “the sharp null hypothesis of no effect from the PSAs (during the week they air or in subsequent weeks)”) and randomization inference (p. 172: “one may simulate the sampling distribution of possible estimated treatment effects under all possible random assignments. The $p$ value of the observed estimate is calculated based on its location relative to this randomization distribution”). Not in the paper and defined by the validator (P024-A002/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 3–6): the onset $S$ and its distribution, the exposure indicator $Z_t(s)$, the potential-outcome schedule $Y_t(s)$, the estimand $\tau$ (the average, over the two periods with $0 < p_t < 1$, of the within-period effect), the inverse-probability estimator $\widehat{\tau}$, the before-after statistic $D$ (mean outcome from the onset on, minus mean outcome before it) and the upper-tail randomization $p$-value.
canonical_claim.note: Finding P024-A002 is rated Moderate; the validator's verdict is confirmed_in_part, upheld on re-run: the necessity claim is false for the randomized-timing design the paragraph has just introduced (this witness), while a narrower reading, a caution against treating a raw before-after change as the effect, is sound and is part (c) of P024-T2. The witness needs only exact rational arithmetic over three equally likely onsets. All numbers above were recomputed in exact arithmetic when this list was fixed and agree with P024-A002/v1/artifact/check-output.txt. Periods 1 and 4 are left out of $\tau$ because $p_1 = 0$ and $p_4 = 1$. The artifact also checks the fresh reader's six-period witness ($S$ uniform on $\{2, \ldots, 6\}$, $Y_t(0) = 10t + 3t^2$, $Y_t(1) = Y_t(0) + 2$, estimand over periods 2 to 5; estimates $2505/16$, $1665/16$, $695/16$, $-785/16$, $-245$ with mean 2; null statistics 81, 87, 93, 99, 105 with $p$-values $1$, $4/5$, $3/5$, $2/5$, $1/5$); it is the same argument and is not a separate target. What a proof establishes: a no-trend condition is not necessary for design-based estimation or for sharp-null inference under randomized timing. What it does not establish: that a realized estimate is close to the truth (the variance is $1561/8$), that the test has useful power (it cannot reject at any level below $1/3$), or which reading the authors intended.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Single-Medium Multi-Outcome Crossover Design’, first paragraph, sentence beginning ‘In order to attribute a change in outcomes to the treatment’, as repaired by Sol
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P024-A002, prior_correction.corrected_text; smallest_repair gives the same repair as an instruction). It replaces the sentence “In order to attribute a change in outcomes to the treatment, one must assume that the treatment is the sole systematic factor that changes over time.” Verbatim: “An unadjusted before-after change can reflect other factors that vary over time. With a known randomization mechanism, randomized timing can support design-based effect estimation and sharp-null randomization inference despite fixed calendar trends. Effect estimation must specify the estimand, ensure the relevant assignment probabilities are positive, and address treatment history, anticipation, and carryover in its estimand or assumptions.”
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (validator derivation, sections 4–6). [Setting] One unit (one media outlet) observed in periods $t = 1, \ldots, T$. A finite set $\Omega$ of treatment schedules with a known probability distribution; schedule $\omega$ gives exposure indicators $Z_t(\omega) \in \{0, 1\}$ (in the validator's case $\Omega$ is a set of onsets and $Z_t(s) = \mathbf{1}\{t \ge s\}$). The schedule is the only randomness and all outcomes are observed.
(a) [Design-based estimation despite a fixed calendar trend.] Hypotheses: fixed real numbers $Y_t(0)$ and $Y_t(1)$ for each period, with no restriction on how either varies with $t$; the observed outcome under schedule $\omega$ is $Y_t = Y_t(Z_t(\omega))$ (the outcome depends on the schedule only through current exposure: no anticipation, no carryover, no dependence on duration); $p_t = \Pr(Z_t = 1)$; the set $E = \{t : 0 < p_t < 1\}$ is nonempty. Conclusion: $$\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1}{|E|}\sum_{t \in E}\left\{\frac{Z_tY_t}{p_t} - \frac{(1 - Z_t)Y_t}{1 - p_t}\right\}\right] = \frac{1}{|E|}\sum_{t \in E}[Y_t(1) - Y_t(0)].$$ No independence of the $Z_t$ across periods is used.
(b) [Sharp-null randomization inference despite a fixed calendar trend.] Hypotheses: $\Omega$ has $m \ge 1$ schedules, each with probability $1/m$; under the sharp null the outcome path $y = (y_1, \ldots, y_T)$ is the same under every schedule and is otherwise arbitrary; $D(\omega) = D(\omega; y)$ is any real-valued statistic; $p(\omega) = \#\{\upsilon \in \Omega : D(\upsilon) \ge D(\omega)\}/m$. Conclusion: for the realized schedule $W$, uniform on $\Omega$, $\Pr(p(W) \le \alpha) \le \alpha$ for every $\alpha \in [0, 1]$.
(c) [An unadjusted before-after change can reflect other factors.] In the population of P024-T1 with no effect ($Y_t(s) = t^2$ for every $s$) and $S$ uniform on $\{2, 3, 4\}$, the before-after statistic $D$ of P024-T1 has $\mathrm{E}[D(S)] = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{26}{3} + 10 + \frac{34}{3}\right) = 10 \ne 0$. With the constant effect 2 restored ($Y_t(s) = t^2 + 2\,\mathbf{1}\{t \ge s\}$) the same statistic takes the value $D(s) + 2$ for each onset and has expectation $12 \ne 2$. Randomizing the onset does not make the raw before-after difference unbiased for the effect.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P024-T1. The sentence being replaced and its paragraph are transcribed in P024-T3. ‘Fixed calendar trend’: the untreated outcomes $Y_t(0)$ (in (b), the null path $y$) vary with $t$ and are fixed before the schedule is drawn. ‘Design-based’: expectations and probabilities are over the known distribution of the schedule only. ‘The relevant assignment probabilities are positive’: the estimand of (a) averages over the periods in $E$, where both exposure states have positive probability. These glosses are the validator's (P024-A002/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 3–6); the paper has no corresponding definitions.
canonical_claim.note: Repair cost recorded by Sol: weaker_conclusion. The blanket necessity claim becomes a warning about unadjusted attribution, and the local reason for calling the multi-message design ‘stronger’ cannot rest on a no-trend requirement; the multi-message design, its randomization tests and the before-after caution stand. Parts (a) and (b) are the general forms the validator states after its numerical witness (“the identity holds for any fixed potential outcomes satisfying the specified current-exposure mapping and overlap”; “the same conclusion holds for any fixed outcome path”). (a) is linearity of expectation with $\mathrm{E}[Z_t] = p_t$; (b) is the standard validity argument for a randomization test in which ties count against rejection. P024-T1 (ii) and (iii) are their instances with $T = 4$ and three onsets, so the proofs should share definitions. The values in (c) were recomputed exactly when this list was fixed. Part (b) also carries the formal content of the article's statements that randomization inference may be used: p. 172 (transcribed in standing_assumptions) and, for the six-organization design with $6! = 720$ equally likely orderings, p. 174 (headline claim P024-H7). Those sentences describe a procedure and are not separate targets. The third sentence of the corrected text is guidance on what an analysis must specify and has no further formal content; in (a) it appears as the hypotheses (current-exposure mapping, $E$ nonempty). Not asserted: that the multi-message design has no advantage in precision or robustness, or that effects can be estimated without a stated exposure mapping.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Between-Subjects Clustered Design’, second paragraph, sentence ‘The difference-in-means estimator is consistent, which is to say that it converges to the correct answer as the number of clusters becomes very large’, as printed; the witness is the validator's construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement refuted: p. 171 (PDF p. 5)] “The difference-in-means estimator is consistent, which is to say that it converges to the correct answer as the number of clusters becomes very large, but bias may be appreciable in studies with only a few dozen clusters of varying size.” [Reading refuted] Under clustered assignment with the article's conditions (a)–(c) and a common assignment probability, the individual-level difference in means converges in probability to the average treatment effect among all subjects whenever the number of clusters tends to infinity. [Witness: validator's construction, not in the paper] For each integer $K \ge 2$ the population has $K$ clusters: cluster 1 with $n_1 = K^2$ individuals and clusters $2, \ldots, K$ with one individual each, so $N_K = K^2 + K - 1$. Potential outcomes are fixed: every individual in cluster 1 has $Y(0) = 1/2$ and $Y(1) = 3/4$; every singleton has $Y(0) = 1/4$ and $Y(1) = 1/2$. Every individual effect is $1/4$, so the average effect is $\tau_K = 1/4$ for every $K$, and every potential outcome lies in $(0, 1)$. Clusters are assigned as wholes, $Z_j \in \{0, 1\}$; all outcomes are observed and there is no interference. With $\bar{Y}_j(z)$ the mean of $Y(z)$ in cluster $j$, the estimator on allocations with both arms nonempty is $$\widehat{\tau}_K = \frac{\sum_j Z_j n_j \bar{Y}_j(1)}{\sum_j Z_j n_j} - \frac{\sum_j (1 - Z_j) n_j \bar{Y}_j(0)}{\sum_j (1 - Z_j) n_j}.$$ [Claims] (i) [Exact values.] On an allocation with $m$ treated clusters, $1 \le m \le K - 1$: if cluster 1 is treated, $\widehat{\tau}_K = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{K^2}{K^2 + m - 1}$; if cluster 1 is in control, $\widehat{\tau}_K = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{K^2}{K^2 + K - m - 1}$. (ii) [Independent assignment, the design the article describes.] Let $Z_1, \ldots, Z_K$ be independent with $\Pr(Z_j = 1) = 1/2$. On every allocation with both arms nonempty, $$|\widehat{\tau}_K - \tau_K| \ge \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{K^2}{K^2 + K - 2} > \frac{1}{8},$$ and these allocations have total probability $1 - 2^{1-K}$. Hence $\Pr(|\widehat{\tau}_K - \tau_K| > 1/8) \ge 1 - 2^{1-K} \to 1$ as $K \to \infty$, whatever value the estimator is given on the two empty-arm allocations; $\widehat{\tau}_K - \tau_K$ does not converge to 0 in probability. Conditionally on both arms being nonempty, $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau}_K] = 1/4$: the failure is not one of bias. (iii) [Complete randomization of half the clusters.] For even $K$, let the treated set be uniform over the subsets of $K/2$ clusters, and put $r_K = K^2/(K^2 + K/2 - 1)$. Then $\widehat{\tau}_K = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4}r_K$ with probability $1/2$ and $\widehat{\tau}_K = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4}r_K$ with probability $1/2$; $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau}_K] = 1/4$; $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_K) = r_K^2/16 \to 1/16$; and, since $r_K > 1/2$, $\Pr(|\widehat{\tau}_K - \tau_K| > 1/8) = 1$ for every even $K \ge 2$. (iv) [What fails.] The largest cluster's share of the population is $n_1/N_K = K^2/(K^2 + K - 1) \to 1$. (v) [Instance $K = 6$.] Cluster sizes $(36, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)$. Under (iii) the 20 equally likely allocations give $37/76$ ten times and $1/76$ ten times, with variance $81/1444$. Under (ii), 62 of the 64 allocations have both arms nonempty and the smallest absolute error among them is $9/40$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: clustered assignment (“all individuals living within the same geographic cluster are assigned together to either treatment or control conditions. In the between-subjects clustered design, clusters are assigned independently, but individuals within clusters are not”, p. 171, PDF p. 5); “the standard estimation approach—comparing treatment and control group averages” (p. 171), that is, the average outcome of all individuals in treated clusters minus that of all individuals in control clusters (p. 170, PDF p. 4: “The average outcome in the control group is subtracted from the average outcome in the treatment group”); “the correct answer” is “the average treatment effect among all subjects” (p. 171), the “\emph{individual-level} average treatment effect” (p. 172, PDF p. 6); “consistent, which is to say that it converges to the correct answer as the number of clusters becomes very large” (p. 171). The article's conditions (a)–(c) (p. 170) are transcribed in standing_assumptions. Not in the paper and supplied by the validator (P024-E002/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 2–4): the sequence of populations indexed by $K$, the potential outcomes, the two assignment mechanisms, and the reading of ‘converges’ as convergence in probability of $\widehat{\tau}_K - \tau_K$ to 0 under the design.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Everything in the statement except three limits is exact for each fixed $K$: the two formulas in (i); in (ii), the inequality $|\widehat{\tau}_K - \tau_K| \ge \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{K^2}{K^2+K-2} > \frac{1}{8}$ on every allocation with both arms nonempty, the probability $1 - 2^{1-K}$ of those allocations and the conditional mean $1/4$; in (iii), the two-point distribution, its mean $1/4$, its variance $r_K^2/16$ and $r_K > 1/2$; and the share in (iv). The only limiting steps are $2^{1-K} \to 0$, $r_K \to 1$ and $K^2/(K^2+K-1) \to 1$. Non-convergence in probability already follows from the finite bound $\Pr(|\widehat{\tau}_K - \tau_K| > 1/8) \ge 1 - 2^{1-K} \ge 1/2$ for every $K \ge 2$ (P024-E002/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 3–4).
canonical_claim.note: Finding P024-E002 is rated Minor (a missing regularity condition), confirmed and upheld on re-run; the brief asks for the validator's counterexample to the printed statement at any severity. (iii) is an additional standard design in which the estimator is exactly unbiased and still inconsistent. Proof sketch from the artifact. (i) is direct substitution: when cluster 1 is treated the control arm consists of singletons with mean $1/4$ and the treated mean is $[(3/4)K^2 + (1/2)(m-1)]/(K^2 + m - 1)$; symmetrically when it is in control. The inequality in (ii) uses that the number of singletons sharing cluster 1's arm is between 0 and $K - 2$, and $\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{K^2}{K^2+K-2} - \frac{1}{8} = \frac{K^2 - K + 2}{8(K^2 + K - 2)} > 0$. Conditional unbiasedness in (ii) holds because an allocation and its complement have the same number of singletons in cluster 1's arm, so their estimates sum to $1/2$. All values were recomputed by exact enumeration at $K = 2, 4, 6, 8$ when this list was fixed and agree with P024-E002/v1/artifact/check-output.txt. The fresh reader's zero-effect witness (outcomes 0 or 1; estimates $\pm 18/19$ at $K = 6$ under (iii)) is checked in the same artifact and is not a separate target. What a proof establishes: a growing number of clusters does not by itself give consistency. What it does not establish: that the estimator is inconsistent under the usual regularity conditions (P024-T5 shows the contrary), that the finite-sample bias warning in the same sentence is wrong, or that any cited application has a dominant cluster.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Between-Subjects Clustered Design’, second paragraph, the consistency sentence, corrected
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's replacement for the consistency clause (validated.json, P024-E002, smallest_repair), verbatim: “With uniformly bounded potential outcomes and a common cluster treatment probability bounded away from zero and one, the difference-in-means estimator is consistent as the number of independently assigned clusters grows, provided that no cluster accounts for a nonvanishing share of all subjects.” Sol adds: “For complete cluster randomization, use a treatment fraction bounded away from zero and one. The no-dominance condition is max_j n_j/N -> 0, equivalently sum_j (n_j/N)^2 -> 0.” The rest of the printed sentence (“but bias may be appreciable in studies with only a few dozen clusters of varying size”) is unchanged.
[Corrected statement in full; validator derivation, section 5] [Setting] A sequence of finite populations indexed by $K = 2, 3, \ldots$ The $K$-th population has $K$ clusters with sizes $n_j \ge 1$ ($j = 1, \ldots, K$), $N = \sum_j n_j$ individuals, and fixed potential outcomes $Y_{ij}(0)$, $Y_{ij}(1)$ for individual $i$ of cluster $j$; sizes and outcomes may change with $K$. Put $w_j = n_j/N$, $\bar{Y}_j(z) = n_j^{-1}\sum_i Y_{ij}(z)$, $\mu_z = \sum_j w_j\bar{Y}_j(z)$ and $\tau_K = \mu_1 - \mu_0$, the average treatment effect among all individuals. Clusters are assigned as wholes with indicators $Z_j \in \{0,1\}$; every individual's outcome is observed and equals $Y_{ij}(Z_j)$ (no interference, assignment implemented as planned). The estimator is $$\widehat{\tau}_K = \frac{\sum_j Z_j n_j \bar{Y}_j(1)}{\sum_j Z_j n_j} - \frac{\sum_j (1 - Z_j) n_j \bar{Y}_j(0)}{\sum_j (1 - Z_j) n_j}$$ when both arms are nonempty, and any real number otherwise.
[Hypotheses] (i) [Bounded outcomes] there is $B < \infty$, not depending on $K$, with $|Y_{ij}(z)| \le B$ for all $K$, $j$, $i$, $z$. (ii) [Design] either $Z_1, \ldots, Z_K$ are independent with a common probability $\Pr(Z_j = 1) = p_K$, or the treated set is uniform over the subsets of $m_K$ clusters and $p_K = m_K/K$. (iii) [Interior probability] there is $\eta > 0$, not depending on $K$, with $\eta \le p_K \le 1 - \eta$. (iv) [No dominant cluster] $\max_j w_j \to 0$ as $K \to \infty$.
[Conclusion] For every $\epsilon > 0$, $\Pr(|\widehat{\tau}_K - \tau_K| > \epsilon) \to 0$ as $K \to \infty$. Neither $\tau_K$ nor $p_K$ is required to converge.
[Equivalent form of (iv)] $\max_j w_j \to 0$ if and only if $\sum_j w_j^2 \to 0$.
[What does not hold] Hypotheses (i)–(iii) and $K \to \infty$ without (iv) do not imply the conclusion: P024-T4.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P024-T4. Conditions (i)–(iv), the weights $w_j$, the normalized totals $A = \sum_j Z_j w_j \bar{Y}_j(1)$ and $C = \sum_j (1 - Z_j) w_j \bar{Y}_j(0)$ and the treated share $D = \sum_j Z_j w_j$ (so that $\widehat{\tau}_K = A/D - C/(1 - D)$ when $0 < D < 1$) are the validator's (P024-E002/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 5), not the paper's. ‘Consistent’ is read as the paper glosses it (“converges to the correct answer as the number of clusters becomes very large”, p. 171, PDF p. 5), made precise as convergence in probability of $\widehat{\tau}_K - \tau_K$ to 0 under the design.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact statements for one population with $K$ clusters ($K \ge 2$ under complete randomization), on which the limit rests (validator derivation, section 5; P024-E002/recheck-v1/independent-check.md re-derives L1, L2 and L5). L1 [weights]: for $w_j \ge 0$ with $\sum_j w_j = 1$, $(\max_j w_j)^2 \le \sum_j w_j^2 \le \max_j w_j$. L2 [variance of a weighted sum of assignment indicators]: for fixed real $x_1, \ldots, x_K$, under independent assignment with common probability $p$, $\mathrm{Var}(\sum_j Z_j x_j) = p(1-p)\sum_j x_j^2$; under complete randomization of $m$ of $K$ clusters with $p = m/K$, $\mathrm{E}[Z_j] = p$, $\mathrm{Cov}(Z_j, Z_l) = -p(1-p)/(K-1)$ for $j \ne l$, and $\mathrm{Var}(\sum_j Z_j x_j) = p(1-p)\frac{K}{K-1}\left[\sum_j x_j^2 - \frac{(\sum_j x_j)^2}{K}\right] \le p(1-p)\frac{K}{K-1}\sum_j x_j^2$. The same holds with $1 - Z_j$ in place of $Z_j$. L3 [moments of the normalized totals]: $\mathrm{E}[A] = p\mu_1$, $\mathrm{E}[C] = (1-p)\mu_0$, $\mathrm{E}[D] = p$, and, with $c = 1$ for independent assignment and $c = K/(K-1)$ for complete randomization, under (i), $\mathrm{Var}(A) \le \frac{c}{4}B^2\sum_j w_j^2$, $\mathrm{Var}(C) \le \frac{c}{4}B^2\sum_j w_j^2$ and $\mathrm{Var}(D) \le \frac{c}{4}\sum_j w_j^2$. L4 [Chebyshev]: $\Pr(|X - \mathrm{E}X| \ge t) \le \mathrm{Var}(X)/t^2$ for $t > 0$. L5 [ratio bound, deterministic]: if $\eta \le p \le 1 - \eta$, $|\mu_1| \le B$, $|\mu_0| \le B$ and $|D - p| < \eta/2$, then $D \ge \eta/2$, $1 - D \ge \eta/2$, $\left|\frac{A}{D} - \mu_1\right| \le \frac{2}{\eta}\left(|A - p\mu_1| + B|D - p|\right)$ and $\left|\frac{C}{1-D} - \mu_0\right| \le \frac{2}{\eta}\left(|C - (1-p)\mu_0| + B|D - p|\right)$. L6 [finite-sample bound]: let $\epsilon > 0$, $L = \max(B, 1)$ and $\delta = \min\{\eta/2,\ \epsilon\eta/(16L)\}$. If $|A - p\mu_1| \le \epsilon\eta/8$, $|C - (1-p)\mu_0| \le \epsilon\eta/8$ and $|D - p| < \delta$, then both arms are nonempty and $|\widehat{\tau}_K - \tau_K| \le 3\epsilon/4$. Consequently, under (i)–(iii), $$\Pr(|\widehat{\tau}_K - \tau_K| \ge \epsilon) \le \frac{c}{4}\left(\sum_j w_j^2\right)\left[\frac{128B^2}{\epsilon^2\eta^2} + \frac{1}{\delta^2}\right],$$ whatever value the estimator is given on empty-arm allocations; by L1 the right side tends to 0 under (iv).
canonical_claim.note: Repair cost recorded by Sol: minor_regularity_condition; the estimator, the estimand and the conclusion are unchanged on admissible sequences. The conditions are sufficient, not necessary; the validator makes no necessity claim. The common assignment probability matters: the unweighted difference in means is not covered under unequal cluster propensities. The article supplies none of (i)–(iv) and no sampling model. Replication of a fixed set of cluster types, the case the fresh Opus reader checked numerically, satisfies (iv). The index of the sequence is the number of clusters, as in the validator's derivation; (iv) forces the number of clusters to infinity in any case, since $\max_j w_j \ge 1/K$. If the limit statement proves hard to formalize, L6 together with L1 is the whole mathematical content and is the fallback. The single displayed inequality of L6 is this list's assembly of the validator's union-bound and Chebyshev steps, which the derivation gives in words with the same thresholds; it, the variance identities of L2 and the bounds of L3 and L5 were checked by exact enumeration on small random populations under both designs when this list was fixed. This target also covers the consistency clause of headline claim P024-H3; the printed clause is not listed as a separate asymptotic headline target because it is false as printed (P024-T4).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Between-Subjects Design’, first paragraph (unnumbered statement that the difference in group means is unbiased for the average causal effect)
canonical_claim.statement: “The most basic experimental design is one in which subjects are assigned individually and with identical probability to treatment or control conditions. Assuming that (a) the random assignments are implemented as planned and outcomes are observed for all subjects, (b) the only systematic factor that causes the treatment group to differ from the control group is the intended treatment, and (c) subjects respond solely to the treatment that they receive (and are unaffected by treatments administered to others), the between-subjects design provides the basis for unbiased estimation of the average causal effect of the treatment in the subject pool (Gerber & Green, 2012). Indeed, the estimation of the average causal effect is simple and intuitive: The average outcome in the control group is subtracted from the average outcome in the treatment group.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The paper gives the design (“subjects are assigned individually and with identical probability to treatment or control conditions”), the three assumptions (a)–(c) and the estimator (the treatment-group average minus the control-group average) in the words quoted, all on p. 170 (PDF p. 4). It does not define ‘average causal effect’, ‘subject pool’ or ‘unbiased’ formally and gives no notation; it cites Gerber and Green (2012), which is not staged. Standard meanings, as used by both readers: the subject pool is the finite set of $N$ experimental subjects; the average causal effect is $\tau = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]$; unbiased means that the expectation of the estimator over the random assignment equals $\tau$.
canonical_claim.note: The audit's formal reading (the paper has no formula). $N \ge 2$ subjects with fixed potential outcomes $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$ (condition (c): each depends only on the subject's own assignment); the observed outcome is $Y_i = Y_i(Z_i)$ for every subject (condition (a)); the assignment is the only randomness (condition (b)). Design: complete randomization, the treated set uniform over the subsets of size $m$, $1 \le m \le N - 1$, so that every subject has probability $m/N$. Claim: $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1}{m}\sum_i Z_iY_i - \frac{1}{N-m}\sum_i (1-Z_i)Y_i\right] = \tau$. The same holds, with the same proof by linearity, for any assignment distribution under which exactly $m$ subjects are treated with probability one and $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = m/N$ for every $i$. Under independent assignment with a common probability $p \in (0,1)$ the estimator is undefined on the two allocations with an empty arm, and the claim is $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\tau} \mid 1 \le \sum_i Z_i \le N-1] = \tau$, which follows from the fixed-$m$ case by conditioning on $\sum_i Z_i$. ‘Identical probability’ is not sufficient by itself when the number treated is random and related to outcomes; the clustered design of P024-T7 is the article's own example, which is why the reading fixes the design. Both readers report that the claim held up: Opus by exact enumeration for a six-subject population ($Y(0) = (1,4,2,7,3,9)$, $Y(1) = (3,4,6,8,2,15)$, $\tau = 2$) for every $m = 1, \ldots, 5$ and under Bernoulli(1/3) assignment conditional on nonempty arms (runs/P024/fresh-opus/scripts/checks.py, part 1; the fixed-$m$ cases were recomputed when this list was fixed); Sol by derivation from equal inclusion probabilities and by enumeration of the six two-of-four allocations. No confirmed finding touches this statement: P024-E001 concerns a number in the Bond et al. example that follows it, and P024-A001, on Note 1, was not confirmed.
